findings.title: Blocked-email match is case/whitespace sensitive and bypassable
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first with the raw value, while other paths normalize with Email.downcase(...).strip (see UsersController#change_email). An attacker can bypass a block by changing case or adding whitespace, and the uniqueness validation plus unique index on blocked_emails are also case-sensitive so the same address can exist in multiple forms. Normalize (downcase/strip) on write and on lookup.

findings.title: Non-atomic match_count increment with side effect inside validation
findings.body: should_block? does record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = ...; record.save when a record matches, and it is called from EmailValidator#validate_each. That makes every validation attempt perform a read-modify-write DB write, so concurrent signups lose increments, failed validations still inflate statistics, and validation now has a persistent side effect. Use an atomic counter update separated from the boolean check.

findings.title: change_email path bypasses blocked-email validation
findings.body: UsersController#change_email only checks User.where("email = ?", lower_email).exists? and then creates an email_token and sends an authorization email. It never runs User email validation / EmailValidator / BlockedEmail.should_block?, so a blocked address rejected at signup can still be adopted via the email-change flow. Enforce the same block check before creating the token.
